atoms.idea: Example 3.6: SCARA IK. From Example 3.1, the tool pose is a z-rotation by φ at position (x, y, z); we solve for joints given x, y, z, φ (Eq 3.38).
atoms.feynman: Tell the desk lamp where the bulb should be and which way it faces, and figure out the hinge angles.
atoms.visual: SCARA preset with a draggable gold target: a dot in 3D with a heading arrow φ; the target equation tile g_d holds only φ and (x, y, z).

atoms.idea: Applying the kinematics to the tool origin gives p(θ) = (x, y, z); the third component l0 + θ4 = z gives θ4 = z − l0 directly, without any subproblem.
atoms.feynman: The elevator height is simply the target height minus the column height.
atoms.visual: Dragging the gold target up and down moves only the slider joint; a height bar shows θ4 = z − l0; no badge is needed (a small ✓).

atoms.idea: Page number 106.

pages.summary: SCARA IK continued: with θ4 known (Eq 3.39), a distance from axis 1 to axis 3 gives θ2 by Subproblem 3 (Eq 3.40), then θ1 and θ3 by Subproblem 1 (Eq 3.41); at most two solutions.

atoms.label: Fig 3.12
atoms.idea: SCARA at its reference pose (same as Fig 3.3), with the axis points q1, q2, q3.
atoms.feynman: The desk lamp again, stretched straight out.
atoms.visual: SCARA preset home pose with teal axis points q1, q2, q3.

atoms.label: Eq (3.39)
atoms.idea: Move θ4 to the right: exp(ξ̂1θ1)exp(ξ̂2θ2)exp(ξ̂3θ3) = g_d g_st(0)^{-1} exp(−ξ̂4θ4) =: g1.
atoms.feynman: With the elevator height done, only the three swings are left.
atoms.visual: The θ4 tile slides across the equals sign as its inverse and merges into a gold g1 tile; knob 4 locks in orange.

atoms.label: Eq (3.40)
atoms.idea: Apply to p on axis 3, subtract q on axis 1, take norms: ‖exp(ξ̂2θ2)p − q‖ = ‖g1 p − q‖ =: δ. Subproblem 3 gives θ2.
atoms.feynman: How far the end hinge is from the base hinge depends only on the middle hinge bend.
atoms.visual: Teal tape from base axis q to a pin on axis 3: knobs 1 and 3 leave its length fixed; knob 2 changes it; the 📏 badge finds two θ2 values (elbow left/right).

atoms.idea: Then θ1: apply the equation to a point p′ on axis 3 so θ3 drops out, giving exp(ξ̂1θ1)(exp(ξ̂2θ2)p′) = g1 p′: Subproblem 1.
atoms.feynman: Now that the arm bend is known, swing the whole arm at the base until the end hinge is above the target.
atoms.visual: The 🎠 badge swings the pinned axis-3 point around axis 1 onto its gold ghost; knob 1 locks.

atoms.label: Eq (3.41)
atoms.idea: Finally exp(ξ̂3θ3) = exp(−ξ̂2θ2)exp(−ξ̂1θ1)g_d g_st^{-1}exp(−ξ̂4θ4); apply to any point off axis 3 and use Subproblem 1 for θ3.
atoms.feynman: Last, turn the end hinge so the gripper faces the right way.
atoms.visual: A teal point off axis 3 swings onto its gold ghost; the heading arrow at the tool matches φ (lime); knob 3 locks.

atoms.idea: The SCARA has at most two IK solutions, from the two roots of Eq (3.40).
atoms.feynman: The lamp's middle hinge can bend left or right to reach the same spot.
atoms.visual: A two-leaf tree; both ghost SCARAs (left-elbow and right-elbow) touch the gold target together.

atoms.idea: Page number 107.

pages.summary: Subproblems work mainly when axes intersect; for general arms, IK uses elimination theory (dialytic elimination) to reduce n polynomials in n unknowns to one polynomial in one unknown. Example 3.7 sets up three quadratic-type polynomials.

atoms.idea: Subsection 3.4 General solutions to inverse kinematics problems.
The subproblems (and their exercise extensions) decompose IK for many arms, chiefly when some joint axes intersect.
atoms.feynman: The three tools fit most furniture, but only furniture with the right kind of bolts (intersecting axes).
atoms.visual: A gallery of arms: those with intersecting axes get a lime 🧰 badge; an arm with skewed, non-meeting axes gets a coral 🧰✗ badge.

atoms.idea: General IK (no intersecting axes), planar or spatial, was an active research topic at the time: how many solutions there are and how to compute them in real time. A summary of the most general approaches follows.
atoms.feynman: When the bolts don't line up, you need a universal method, and an open question is how many ways the arm could reach a spot at all.
atoms.visual: The skewed-axis arm with a gold target and a "?" counter for the number of solutions.

atoms.idea: These approaches rest on classical elimination theory: systematically eliminate n−1 variables from n polynomials in n unknowns to get one polynomial in one unknown. It is general but brute force, using only simple structure. The technique is called dialytic elimination.
atoms.feynman: Like solving a sudoku by pure bookkeeping: keep combining rows until only one unknown is left in one equation.
atoms.visual: Three equation cards with unknowns x1, x2, x3 drawn as colored beads; an "eliminate" button combines cards until only x1 beads remain on one card.

atoms.label: Ex 3.7
atoms.idea: Example 3.7: three polynomials f1, f2, f3 in x1, x2, x3, each a linear combination (coefficients a_i…g_i) of the monomials x1², x1x2, x1x3, x2², x3, 1.
atoms.feynman: Three shopping receipts, each listing how many of the same six item types were bought; we want the item prices that make all totals zero.
atoms.visual: A 3×6 tile grid of real coefficients multiplying a column of six monomial beads (x1², x1x2, x1x3, x2², x3, 1); result column of three zeros.

atoms.idea: Goal: eliminate x2, x3 to get a single polynomial in x1, in two steps; Step 1 rewrites the system in x2, x3 (continues).
atoms.feynman: First treat x1 as a known number, then only x2 and x3 are unknowns.
atoms.visual: The x1 beads turn into a slider (orange knob); the grid tiles become small polynomials in x1.

atoms.idea: Page number 108.

pages.summary: Dialytic elimination: treat coefficients as polynomials in x1, multiply by x2 to add independent rows until the monomial count equals the equation count, form a square A(x1), and require det A(x1) = 0 (generically degree six); null vectors give x2, x3.

atoms.idea: Step 1: write the system as a 3×4 matrix whose entries are polynomials in x1, multiplying the monomials (x2², x3, x2, 1).
atoms.feynman: Pretend one ingredient's amount is fixed; then the recipe is a smaller table in the remaining ingredients.
atoms.visual: The grid shrinks to 3×4 with tiles that pulse as the x1 slider moves; four monomial beads in x2, x3 on the right.

atoms.idea: Step 2: create more independent polynomials until there are as many equations as unknown monomials. Multiplying f1, f2, f3 by x2 gives three new equations in x2³, x2x3, x2², x2.
atoms.feynman: Making extra clues by doubling: multiply each clue by x2 to get new, different clues about bigger monomials.
atoms.visual: Each row card is cloned and stamped "× x2"; the clone's beads shift up one degree (x2² → x2³, x3 → x2x3 …).

atoms.idea: Combining gives six equations in the six monomials x2³, x2x3, x2², x2, x3, 1: a square 6×6 matrix A(x1) times the monomial vector equals 0.
atoms.feynman: Six clues and six unknown "items": now the puzzle is a square table.
atoms.visual: The 3×4 original and 3×4 clone stack into a 6×6 tile grid (zero tiles in slate) multiplying a six-bead column; a "square ✓" badge appears.

atoms.idea: A nonzero monomial vector (its last entry is 1) can only be in the null space if det A(x1) = 0, so the system is equivalent to det A(x1) = 0, a polynomial in x1, generically of degree six, whose roots need not be real.
atoms.feynman: A squishing machine can only flatten a non-zero arrow to nothing if it squashes space flat: its volume factor (determinant) must be zero.
atoms.visual: Sweep the x1 slider: a plot draws det A(x1) as a blue curve; gold dots mark zero crossings; at each, the 6×6 grid visibly loses rank (a unit cube squashes flat).

atoms.idea: The degree bounds the number of real solutions; for each real root x1, x2 and x3 are read off from the null vector of A(x1) scaled so its last entry is 1.
atoms.feynman: Once you know x1, the flattened direction of the machine tells you the remaining prices directly.
atoms.visual: At a gold root, the teal null-space column appears beside the grid, rescaled so its "1" bead is exactly 1; its x2 and x3 beads give the answer.

atoms.idea: If the null space has dimension greater than one (a repeated root), there may be several (x2, x3) for that x1; the null-space dimension bounds that multiplicity.
atoms.feynman: Sometimes the machine flattens two directions at once, and there is more than one way to fill in the remaining prices.
atoms.visual: At a double root, two teal null vectors appear and a small fan of (x2, x3) options lights up.

atoms.idea: Footnotes: independence is meant over polynomials in x1; a monomial is a single product of powers such as x2x3 or x1³.
atoms.feynman: A bead is one "word" like x2·x3; independent clues are ones you cannot get by mixing the others with x1-flavored multipliers.
atoms.visual: Hovering a bead shows its monomial; hovering a row shows a lime "new information" tick if it is independent of the rows above.

atoms.idea: Page number 109.

pages.summary: Setting up general six-joint IK: write it in DH form, move the θ1, θ2 and θ6 link transforms to the right (Eq 3.43), name the columns of g_d g_{l6 t}^{-1} (Eq 3.44), and treat ci, si as polynomial unknowns so both sides are cubic.

atoms.idea: For a general 6-joint arm, the POE equation exp(ξ̂1θ1)…exp(ξ̂6θ6)g_st(0) = g_d is rewritten in DH form g_{l0 l1}(θ1)…g_{l5 l6}(θ6)g_{l6 t} = g_d, as in Eq (3.6).
atoms.feynman: Use the bookkeeping style that makes the algebra simplest, even if it is less pretty.
atoms.visual: The six-joint arm with no intersecting axes; its POE tile strip flips into a DH card strip (frames on each link).

atoms.label: Eq (3.42)
atoms.idea: Each DH link transform has the standard four-parameter pattern in (φi, αi, ai, di).
atoms.feynman: Every link card is built from the same four-knob template.
atoms.visual: A DH card opens to the four-slider glyph; joint slider orange, the other three slate fixed.

atoms.label: Eq (3.43)
atoms.idea: Rearrange as g_{l2l3}(θ3) g_{l3l4}(θ4) g_{l4l5}(θ5) = g_{l1l2}^{-1}(θ2) g_{l0l1}^{-1}(θ1) g_d g_{l6t}^{-1} g_{l5l6}^{-1}(θ6): the inverses of the θ1, θ2 and θ6 transforms are moved to the right side.
atoms.feynman: Split a long equation down the middle so each side has about the same amount of unknown stuff.
atoms.visual: Cards for θ1, θ2 and θ6 slide across the equals sign and flip to their inverses; the left keeps θ3, θ4, θ5, balancing at three each like a seesaw.

atoms.label: Eq (3.44)
atoms.idea: Write g_d g_{l6t}^{-1} as a 4×4 matrix with rotation columns l, m, n and translation q.
atoms.feynman: The target pose, with the tool offset removed, is just three direction arrows and a position.
atoms.visual: The gold target tile opens to three colored arrows l, m, n (red, green, blue) and a gold position dot q.

atoms.idea: Set ci = cos θi and si = sin θi and treat Eq (3.43) as polynomial in them; each link transform is degree ≤ 1 in its own ci, si, and the rearrangement makes both sides cubic. The elimination then reduces everything to θ3 (continues).
atoms.feynman: Replace every angle by a pair of numbers (cos, sin) living on a circle; then the whole problem is about polynomials, which algebra can grind through.
atoms.visual: Each orange knob turns into a point on a small unit circle with c and s readouts; a degree meter for each side reads 3.

atoms.idea: Page number 110.

pages.summary: Steps 1-2 of the general method: the last two columns of Eq (3.43) do not depend on θ6; equating them gives six equations EQ1-EQ6 (Eq 3.45) in θ1…θ5, with auxiliary quantities built from DH parameters and the target pose.

atoms.idea: The steps are only sketched; full proofs are in the cited papers.
atoms.feynman: A map of the trail, without every rock described.
atoms.visual: A step tracker with eight numbered stones; a small 📄 icon marks that details live elsewhere.

atoms.idea: Step 1: the third and fourth columns of the right side of Eq (3.43) do not depend on θ6; this follows from the explicit inverse of the DH link transform, whose last two columns contain no θ6.
atoms.feynman: Spinning the hand around its own pointing direction doesn't change which way it points or where its base sits.
atoms.visual: Turn knob 6: in the inverse DH card the first two columns flicker while the last two stay frozen (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (3.45)
atoms.idea: Step 2: equating those columns gives six scalar equations EQ1-EQ6 linking c2, s2, c3, s3 with auxiliary quantities f, r (depending on θ4, θ5) and h, n (depending on θ1 and the target).
atoms.feynman: Six balance scales, each with the arm's middle joints on one pan and the base joints plus target on the other.
atoms.visual: Six seesaw icons; the left pan beads are θ3, θ4, θ5 colored, the right pan beads θ1, θ2 and gold target; each balances when the right angles are dialed in.

atoms.idea: The auxiliary quantities f, r, g, m, h, n are explicit products of the ci, si with the DH constants (ai, di, μi = sin αi, λi = cos αi), and the target enters through p, q, r, u, v, w built from l, m, n, q and the last link's parameters.
atoms.feynman: Bookkeeping labels for sub-totals, so the big equations fit on a page.
atoms.visual: Hovering a seesaw bead expands it into a small tree of the c/s and DH constants it is built from.

atoms.idea: Page number 111.

pages.summary: Step 3 regroups EQ1-EQ6 into two vector equations for p and l (Eq 3.46); Step 4 forms 14 equations from p, l, p·p, p·l, p×l and a combination, collected as P(s3,c3)·(θ4,θ5 monomials) = Q·(θ1,θ2 monomials) (Eq 3.47); Step 5 solves for the θ1,θ2 monomials when Q has rank 8.

atoms.label: Eq (3.46)
atoms.idea: Step 3: regroup the six equations as two vector equations for p and l: (rotation in θ2)·h = (DH α2 matrix)(rotation in θ3)·f + const, and similarly with n and r.
atoms.feynman: Pack six scalar scales into two arrow-balances, each comparing a 3D arrow from the base side with one from the wrist side.
atoms.visual: Two pairs of 3D arrows (pink p, blue l) drawn from each side; they overlap (lime) when the angles are right.

atoms.idea: Left sides are linear combinations of 1, c2, s2, c1, s1, c1c2, s1c2, s1s2; right sides combine (with s3, c3 coefficients) 1, c5, s5, c4, s4, c4c5, s4c5, s4s5.
atoms.feynman: Each side is a short shopping list of the same kinds of items, just with different prices.
atoms.visual: Two bead trays: one with eight θ1/θ2 product beads, one with eight θ4/θ5 product beads, each tray colored by joint.

atoms.label: Eq (3.47)
atoms.idea: Step 4: p, l, p·p, p·l, p×l and (p·p)l − 2(p·l)p all keep the same functional form, giving 3+3+1+1+3+3 = 14 equations: P(s3,c3)·[s4s5, s4c5, c4s5, c4c5, s4, c4, s5, c5, 1] = Q·[s1s2, s1c2, c1s2, c1c2, s1, c1, s2, c2], with P 14×9 and Q a constant 14×8 matrix.
atoms.feynman: Mixing clues by dot and cross products creates new clues that still speak the same "language" of beads, so we end up with 14 clues.
atoms.visual: Fourteen row-tiles stack up (colored by origin: p, l, dots, cross, combo); a 14×9 grid P (pulsing with θ3) on the left and a static 14×8 grid Q on the right.

atoms.label: Eq (3.48)
atoms.idea: Step 5: if rank Q = 8, use 8 of the 14 equations to express the eight θ1,θ2 monomials in terms of the θ4,θ5 monomials; substituting into the other six gives Σ(c3,s3)·[θ4,θ5 monomials] = 0 (continues).
atoms.feynman: Use eight clues to remove the base-joint unknowns entirely; six clues remain, involving only the middle and wrist joints.
atoms.visual: Q's eight columns light up and are "solved away" (beads fade); the remaining six rows form a new 6×9 grid Σ, pulsing with θ3.

atoms.idea: Page number 112.

pages.summary: Rank-deficient Q is deferred to the literature; Step 6 substitutes the tangent half-angle xi = tan(θi/2) to make equations polynomial (Eq 3.49); Step 7 multiplies by x4 to build a 12×12 dialytic system Σ̄ (Eq 3.50).

atoms.idea: Σ(c3, s3) is a 6×9 matrix.
atoms.feynman: Six clues about nine bead types.
atoms.visual: The Σ grid shows its size badge 6×9.

atoms.idea: If Q has rank k < 8, only k of the θ1,θ2 monomials can be eliminated, leaving six equations in more unknowns; details are in the cited paper.
atoms.feynman: If some clues repeat each other, you cannot remove all unknowns, and a harder route is needed.
atoms.visual: Rank slider on Q: below 8 some columns stay lit (coral) and a "harder path" sign appears.

atoms.idea: Step 6: with Q of rank 8, substitute si = 2xi/(1+xi²), ci = (1−xi²)/(1+xi²), with xi = tan(θi/2), for i = 3, 4, 5.
atoms.feynman: Every point on a circle can be reached by a straight line through the circle's bottom point: the slope of that line (half-angle tangent) labels the point without sines or cosines.
atoms.visual: A unit circle with a line from its bottom point (−1) to the point at angle θ; the line hits a vertical ruler at x = tan(θ/2); dragging θ slides x (orange), and c, s readouts are rational functions of x.

atoms.label: Eq (3.49)
atoms.idea: Clear denominators by multiplying by (1+x4²)(1+x5²), and the first four equations also by (1+x3²): Σ1(x3)·[x4²x5², x4²x5, x4², x4x5², x4x5, x4, x5², x5, 1] = 0. The first four rows are quadratic in x3; the last two are rational in x3 but any 6×6 minor is a polynomial in x3 (stated, needs proof).
atoms.feynman: Multiply every clue by the same positive amounts to clear the fractions, like multiplying a recipe by the common denominator.
atoms.visual: Fraction bars on the tiles vanish one by one as (1+x²) factors are multiplied in; the bead column becomes nine products of x4, x5 powers.

atoms.label: Eq (3.50)
atoms.idea: Step 7: dialytic elimination of x4, x5: multiply the six equations by x4 and stack with the originals to get a 12×12 system Σ̄ = [Σ1 0; 0 Σ1] (with 6×3 zero blocks) times 12 monomials equal to 0.
atoms.feynman: The same trick as the small example: clone every clue with an extra x4 until the table is square.
atoms.visual: The 6×9 grid clones itself, shifts three columns to the right (slate zero blocks fill the gaps), and the pair locks into a 12×12 square; a "square ✓" badge.

atoms.idea: Page number 113.

pages.summary: Step 8: det Σ̄ = 0 is a degree-16 polynomial in x3; back-substitute for the other angles and finish θ6 with Subproblem 1. Sixteen is a sharp upper bound for 6R arms (Lee and Liang); numerical drawbacks motivate a generalized eigenvalue formulation (Manocha and Canny).

atoms.idea: Step 8: det Σ̄ = 0 is a polynomial of degree 16 in x3. Solve for x3, then x4, x5 from the null space of Σ̄, then θ1, θ2 from Eq (3.47).
atoms.feynman: Find the special values of one knob where the giant machine flattens; then everything else drops out like dominoes.
atoms.visual: Sweep the x3 slider: a blue curve det Σ̄(x3) with up to 16 gold zero crossings; tapping one shows the teal null vector giving x4, x5, then θ1, θ2 lock in orange.

atoms.idea: Only θ6 remains: with the others known, apply the POE equation to any point p to get exp(ξ̂6θ6)p = q, solved by Subproblem 1.
atoms.feynman: The last hand-roll is the same carousel puzzle as before.
atoms.visual: The 🎠 badge appears at the wrist; a teal point swings onto its gold target; knob 6 locks.

atoms.idea: The procedure gives a 16th-order polynomial in x3, which may or may not have 16 real roots. The elbow arm had at most 8 solutions, but if its wrist axes do not meet, it can have up to 16.
atoms.feynman: A wrist with misaligned bolts can reach the same cup in more ways than a neat one.
atoms.visual: Elbow-arm preset with a "wrist offset" slider: at zero offset the root counter shows ≤8; adding offset reveals more real roots on the curve, up to 16 ghost arms.

atoms.idea: Sixteen is the sharp upper bound for any 6-joint open-chain spatial arm (it is attained), far better than naive Bezout bounds; Lee and Liang first found these tricks (notably the rearrangement of Eq 3.43), settling earlier wrong conjectures.
atoms.feynman: Sixteen is the most ways any six-hinge arm can hold one pose, and there really are arms that use all sixteen.
atoms.visual: A fan of 16 ghost arms all touching one gold pose for a special arm; a counter shows "16 / 16"; a comparison bar shows the much larger naive bound shrinking to 16.

atoms.idea: Drawbacks: mostly numerical (determinants of ill-conditioned matrices), plus conceptual ones such as the rank < 8 case in Step 5 leading to overdetermined systems.
atoms.feynman: Computing a giant determinant is like balancing a tower of many cards: tiny errors can topple it.
atoms.visual: A conditioning meter next to the 12×12 grid: as x3 approaches some values, it turns coral and the det curve jitters with noise.

atoms.idea: Recasting dialytic elimination as a generalized eigenvalue problem improves conditioning and speed, which matters for real-time IK, e.g. for obstacle avoidance in clutter.
atoms.feynman: Instead of balancing the tall card tower, use a sturdy machine that finds all answers at once.
atoms.visual: An "eigen" button replaces the jittery det curve with clean gold eigenvalue dots on the x3 axis; a stopwatch shows faster solve; the arm dodges slate obstacles using the solutions in real time.

atoms.idea: Page number 114.
